q: Why are published studies currently unable to identify definitive behavioural risk factors for dog surrender?
o: Unwanted behaviours occur just as commonly in dogs living successfully in homes as in those being surrendered, so the baseline prevalence in the general pet population is often ignored
Most shelters do not track behavioural data at the time of intake
Behavioural traits are entirely dependent on whether the animal was received as a gift
Dogs consistently express identical behavioural profiles regardless of husbandry changes or new environments
e: Without knowing prevalence in retained homes, you cannot tell whether a behaviour raises surrender risk or is simply common across all pet dogs.

q: A Japanese pet-supply company survey revealed what unexpected reality about pet dog behaviour in successful homes?
o: Fewer than 5% of owners reported any issues with their dogs
Exactly 48% of owners reported severe, unprovoked aggression
No less than 86% of respondents reported at least one troublesome behaviour, with barking and pica causing the most concern
Dogs obtained as gifts displayed zero troublesome behaviours compared with those from breeders
e: The survey showed 86% of successful owners navigate troublesome behaviours (often barking and pica) without ending the relationship.

q: What happens to the odds ratio for daily or weekly inappropriate elimination once a multivariate analysis controls for training, veterinary visits, sterilisation, and work expectations?
o: The risk increases by 200%, proving it is an isolated behavioural issue
The odds ratio is reduced by about 50%, and other behavioural variables become not statistically significant
The variable shifts to predict future inter-cat aggression
The statistical significance remains completely unaltered
e: Adjusting for human and care variables cut the relative risk by about half, showing how confounders distort raw behavioural statistics.

q: What is the predictive value of a relinquishing owner's report of their dog's behaviour for how the dog behaves in a new adoptive home?
o: Excellent predictive value, matching subsequent accounts over 95% of the time
High predictive value, but only for intact male dogs under one year of age
Accurate for house-soiling but completely invalid for barking
Poor predictive value, leaving open whether dogs change behaviour across environments or owners simply vary in perception and definition
e: Owner reports predict poorly because behaviour shifts across environments and definitions of a problem behaviour vary between people.

q: Which parameter was found to significantly increase a shelter dog's likelihood of adoption?
o: Maintaining proximity to the person and engaging in play (fetch or tug) when invited
Approaching the front of the kennel or making direct eye contact with visitors
Vocalising or barking loudly as a release for excitement and frustration
Remaining completely motionless at the back of the enclosure
e: Physical appearance drives initial choice, but proximity and play with the adopter are what statistically boost adoption.

q: During a meet-and-greet, how did experimenters actively promote proximity between a prospective adopter and a shelter dog?
o: They withheld food for 24 hours before the interaction
They placed a visual barrier between dog and adopter for the first 15 minutes
They auditioned dogs for toy preferences, supplied the preferred toy to the adopter, and gave them the leash to hold
They left the adopter alone in an outdoor elimination space with no instructions
e: Auditioning toy preference, supplying the toy, and handing over the leash kept the adopter and dog in close contact.

q: What is the primary mechanism behind chronic indoor elimination developing within a shelter kennel?
o: A rapid increase in territorial behaviour caused by sterilisation
Limited space and lack of outdoor time cause habituation, so the dog loses its natural aversion to eliminating near eating and sleeping areas
Frustration-driven negative reinforcement from passing kennel walkers
Severe intraspecies social deprivation triggering a drop in caloric intake
e: Confinement and inadequate turnout force soiling of the immediate living space, breaking down natural cleanliness and erasing prior training.

q: A kennelled dog barks and lunges whenever other dogs walk past. Through what learning mechanism is this strengthened?
o: Positive reinforcement via a high-value treat schedule
Habituation to the concrete and dirt substrates of the kennel
Classical conditioning linked to a hiding box
Negative reinforcement, because the passing dog continues away, relieving the dog's frustration and rewarding the display
e: The passing stimulus inevitably leaves, relieving frustration and reinforcing the barking through negative reinforcement.

q: How is barking and lunging at passing dogs in a kennel ward best addressed?
o: Visual barriers to prevent exposure that cannot lead to social interaction, plus playgroups or group social walks
Opening all kennel grates to allow maximum face-to-face visual exposure
Confining the dogs in small crates inside a completely silent room
Hand-delivering high-value rewards only when the dog jumps and mouths the gate
e: Passive interventions (visual barriers) stop the frustration trigger, while playgroups and social walks meet the dog's social needs.

q: A volunteer always ignores a dog that jumps and mouths during greetings, yet the behaviour persists. Why does it remain reinforced?
o: The dog is expressing an involuntary skeletal reflex caused by ambient noise
The behaviour is driven by a lack of access to preferred plush toys
Even when ignored, the dog is still rewarded with the most exciting event of its day: being taken out of the kennel
The walker is accidentally changing substrates from concrete to dirt too quickly
e: The outing itself is the reinforcer, so ignoring the jump does not remove the reward that maintains it.

q: When training a dog to stop jumping by walking out of sight for 10 to 15 seconds, what determines the speed of learning?
o: Giving a low-dose behaviour medication before the walker appears
The contingency must be applied consistently; every exception requires more trials to regain lost ground
Maintaining close eye contact with the dog while exiting
Applying the protocol only first thing in the morning
e: Consistency is essential; allowing exceptions reverts the dog to an intermittent schedule and erases progress.

q: What substrate should an outdoor elimination space for shelter dogs provide?
o: Identical concrete flooring to the indoor kennel to promote habituation
Open wire-mesh to maximise visual contact with passing dogs
A single elevated plastic perch
Both dirt and concrete, because dogs form strong associations with the substrate from their previous homes
e: Offering both dirt and concrete matches whatever substrate the dog associates with elimination and supports outdoor success.

q: In environments with high human disturbance, mammals generally show what behavioural shift?
o: A general tendency to increase nocturnal activity across habitats, taxa, and types of human activity
A significant increase in daytime exploratory and predatory behaviour
A complete deactivation of sympathetic nervous system feedback loops
An expansion of home ranges to remain closer to high-volume urban traffic
e: Broad multi-taxa data show that high human disturbance pushes mammals toward nocturnal activity.

q: A collar-mounted camera study (as reported in your notes) found what about hunting habits and success?
o: Cats achieved a 100% success rate when targeting adult birds
Cats killed an average of 45 animals per 24 hours regardless of habitat
73% of hunting occurred between dusk and dawn, and females and night-hunting cats were more successful at killing prey
Hunting occurred exclusively during peak daylight near human housing
e: Per your notes, most hunting was dusk to dawn, with females and night hunters more successful. Note the figures are flagged for verification against the primary source.

q: Which subset of outdoor cats achieved the lowest hunting success rate?
o: Cats hunting mice and rats in semi-desert landscapes
Cats attempting to kill birds, succeeding only 17% of the time
Cats hunting at night near undeveloped habitats
Spayed female cats operating around structured feeding stations
e: Cats were least successful on birds (about 17%); night hunting near undeveloped habitat was actually the more successful pattern.

q: What is an unintended consequence of uncoordinated, pulsed, or short-term lethal control of community cats?
o: An immediate and permanent collapse of local rodent populations
A dramatic reduction in seasonal vegetation variation
An immediate shift in feline activity from nocturnal to crepuscular
Compensatory migration, where removal lets new animals move into the vacated area while resources remain
e: Removal vacates territory while food and shelter persist, so nearby cats migrate in (compensatory migration).

q: Removing community cats can trigger a mesopredator release. What does this imply for native birds?
o: Cat removal can cause a spike in prey species (rats, mice, rabbits) that may worsen survival pressure on native birds
Bird survival immediately doubles due to the absence of mammalian predators
Surviving birds shift to nesting exclusively on concrete substrates
Local predators stop hunting entirely due to reduced resource competition
e: Releasing lower prey species from predation can increase rodents and paradoxically harm the very birds the cull intended to protect.

q: Which group of outdoor cats had the smallest home ranges and the highest population densities?
o: Managed community cats that underwent TNR and were fed on a schedule
Cats far from human housing that were highly nocturnal and lived in small groups
Cats found near houses, crepuscular, largely thought to be owned cats allowed outside during the day
Intact female cats in heavily vegetated landscapes with zero seasonal variation
e: Owned cats let out by day stayed close to structures, giving small ranges and high densities near homes.

q: What spatial and activity profile was observed in the smallest groups of outdoor cats?
o: The smallest home ranges and high activity during peak daylight
They had the largest home ranges, were more nocturnal, and were found farther from human housing
Clustered exclusively near houses on strictly crepuscular schedules
They ceased all hunting and relied entirely on human feeders
e: The smallest, unmanaged groups adapted with the largest ranges, nocturnal activity, and avoidance of human housing.

q: How does the physical presence of the human caretaker affect feline feeding dynamics?
o: Cats flee immediately and refuse to eat for an average of 12 minutes
Feline aggression spikes, disrupting the established colony hierarchy
The cats completely alter their preferred spatial organisation around the station
Cats eat more and stay longer when the person is present (about 4 minutes) than when absent (about 12 seconds)
e: A present feeder is associated with longer, larger feeding bouts (4 minutes vs 12 seconds), changing spatial behaviour at the site.

q: Why should community-cat caretakers set a fixed feeding schedule and remain present while cats eat?
o: It increases the likelihood that cats eat promptly, decreasing the risk of attracting pest species to the feeding area
It expands the cats' home range away from human housing
It induces disinhibition that makes the cats easier to trap for research
It causes an immediate cessation of nocturnal hunting
e: Staying present ensures prompt eating and leaves no scraps to draw rodents or other pests.

q: What behavioural change was confirmed in dominant community cats after successful sterilisation?
o: They completely lost their hierarchy position and the colony collapsed
They shifted from crepuscular activity to strictly diurnal schedules
They were more likely to show less aggression and more affiliative behaviour, and urine spraying decreased dramatically or stopped
They increased their daily distances travelled to expand the colony's range
e: Sterilisation reduced aggression and spraying and increased affiliative behaviour while the overall hierarchy stayed similar.

q: Which community cat should generally NOT be admitted into an animal shelter enclosure?
o: A well-socialised pet cat whose outdoor habitat was destroyed by an emergency demolition
Community cats thriving where they are, not in danger from unusual events, and not impacting vulnerable wildlife
An offensively aggressive adult cat that needs immediate medical triage for a severe injury
A kitten under two months of age meeting the criteria for a socialisation programme
e: Thriving, healthy community cats facing no immediate threat do not belong in a shelter; admitting them strains resources without improving their outcome.

q: The Tiny Spirit programme was designed to address what operational challenge?
o: Managing older cats that develop acute hepatic necrosis from oral medication
Senior kennelled dogs that develop barrier frustration and tail-chasing
Preventing compensatory migration among free-roaming cats near undeveloped habitats
Kittens (about 2 lb (0.9 kg), about 2 months) that show aggression, do well in foster, but regress to defensive, unsocialised behaviour back in the shelter
e: The programme targets undersocialised kittens that plateau and regress when returned to a standard shelter environment.

q: Where does the Tiny Spirit programme place undersocialised kitten kennels to speed habituation and maximise visibility?
o: In the busiest public part of the facility, positioned off the ground at eye level
In an isolated, low-traffic basement ward with minimal lighting
Hand-carried continuously by a single foster volunteer for 14 consecutive days
Directly adjacent to a high-volume canine runway for interspecies habituation
e: Eye-level placement in the busiest area gives continuous passive exposure to people, forcing rapid habituation.

q: What micro-environmental feature is provided inside a Tiny Spirit kitten's enclosure to balance exposure with stress management?
o: A completely transparent glass door left unlocked 24 hours a day
A wire-mesh sub-floor elevated above a concrete drainage canal
A small hiding box about 2 inches (5.1 cm) high
A device playing continuous loud music at 120 dB
e: A low hiding box lets the kitten conceal itself to manage stress while staying low enough to remain visible and accessible.

q: During the first 48 hours of the Tiny Spirit protocol, what rule governs human access and cage doors?
o: Kennel doors are left wide open to encourage exploration of the facility
Kennel doors are locked except for cleaning and structured staff interaction
The kittens are housed in large communal rooms
Adopters are encouraged to handle the kittens without counsellor supervision
e: Locked doors for the first 48 hours give a controlled environment, protecting the kitten from random disruption during early socialisation.

q: What interaction method is used to socialise defensive kittens during the initial 48 hours?
o: Delivering treats via an automated dispenser every 30 seconds
Ignoring all activity until the kitten stops hissing for a full 24-hour cycle
Placing the kitten inside an active playgroup with adult unsterilised cats
A toothbrush on a tongue depressor, 1 minute at a time, 10 times a day, plus burrito wrapping and cheek stroking
e: High-frequency, low-intensity sessions with a toothbrush, plus gentle wrapping and handling, build safe contact.

q: How is positive reinforcement applied during Tiny Spirit socialisation sessions?
o: Handlers deliver a piece of raw meat immediately after the kitten vocalises
Handlers play an audiobook at conversational volume for 15 minutes
Handlers leave the kitten alone immediately after it relaxes
Handlers transfer the kitten directly into an outdoor dirt elimination space
e: Removing the interaction the moment the kitten relaxes uses relief as the reinforcer for calmer behaviour.

q: If a Tiny Spirit kitten makes no clear progress after the first 48 hours, what action is required?
o: Re-evaluate the kitten for the programme, aiming to adopt out, or sterilise and return, within 2 weeks
Double the daily toothbrushing trials to 20 per day indefinitely
Confine the kitten permanently in an isolated wire kennel with zero human access
Move the kennel onto the floor of a high-volume canine housing ward
e: Kittens that stall are re-evaluated promptly to ensure adoption, or sterilisation and return, within a strict 2-week window.
